tabimorelin.text: Listed alongside other growth hormone secretagogues, tabimorelin is discussed as an oral route to higher growth hormone and thereby better body composition. It was studied in a few early human trials for hormone release, and no appearance or body-composition outcome has been tested.

ghrp-1.text: GHRP-1 is an early growth hormone releasing peptide that bodybuilding and peptide communities group with GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 as a way to raise growth hormone for muscle and fat loss. Some 1990s human work measured hormone release; body-composition or appearance outcomes have not been tested.

alexamorelin.text: Alexamorelin is an obscure hexarelin-related peptide that appears in growth hormone secretagogue lists, where the draw is more growth hormone for muscle and fat loss. A 2000 study reported its endocrine effects in humans, and it is mostly known from anti-doping screening; appearance outcomes are untested.

chain: Change in puberty-linked growth and looks
deslorelin.text: Deslorelin is a veterinary GnRH-agonist implant that appears on hormone-focused lists because GnRH agonists shift sex-hormone output. Pediatric endocrine research on related drugs exists, while use of deslorelin itself for appearance is untested and rests on anecdote.

ganirelix.text: Ganirelix is an IVF drug that rapidly suppresses LH and FSH, which is why it is mentioned in hormone-manipulation discussions in muscle and physique circles. Its appearance use is theoretical and untested, with the clinical evidence all coming from fertility treatment.

humanin.text: Humanin is promoted in longevity circles as a mitochondrial peptide that could slow aging, which people connect to staying youthful-looking. The research is in cells and animals, with no human treatment trials and nothing testing skin or other visible aging.

dihexa.text: Dihexa is an experimental peptide taken up by nootropic users for memory and learning, which some tie to study and work performance. It has been studied in rodents for memory, has no published human trials, and no appearance link has been tested.

selank.text: Forum users group selank with Semax as an anxiolytic nootropic for calmer social situations and better focus, which they connect to a more confident presence. Human evidence is a handful of Russian-language studies on anxiety, and appearance effects have not been studied.

cerebrolysin.text: Cerebrolysin is an injectable peptide mixture approved for stroke and dementia in many countries, and forum users discuss it as an iqmaxxing nootropic for study performance. Trials address stroke and dementia, while any appearance link is not drawn or tested.

noopept-omberacetam.text: Noopept is taken as a nootropic for memory, focus and mood, and in appearance forums it appears in stacks aimed at productivity. Small human studies exist for cognition, and no appearance outcome has been tested.

coluracetam.text: Coluracetam is a racetam sold as a nootropic for focus and mood, drawing on its development for Alzheimer's and depression. Appearance use is not drawn by users, and its evidence base is the abandoned pharma programs.

fasoracetam.text: Fasoracetam is a never-marketed racetam that nootropic users take for focus and attention, following its trials in ADHD. It has no appearance angle tested; its place on the wiki is as part of the nootropic stack.

nefiracetam.text: Nefiracetam is a Japanese racetam studied for dementia and post-stroke apathy, and nootropic users take it for memory and drive. Appearance outcomes are untested and not a stated goal.

sunifiram.text: Sunifiram is an unapproved nootropic that users take for learning and focus, based on animal studies showing strong antiamnesic effects. There are no human trials, and no appearance use has been studied.

unifiram.text: Unifiram is the parent compound of sunifiram and is sold online as a potent nootropic for memory and focus. Evidence is limited to animal studies, with no human trials or appearance data.

modafinil.text: Forum users take modafinil to stay alert, study and work longer, and some claim it raises charisma or social ability. It is approved for sleepiness in narcolepsy, sleep apnea and shift work; the appearance and charisma claims are anecdotal and untested.

armodafinil.text: Armodafinil is the longer-acting form of modafinil and is used in the same way, for alertness and productivity in nootropic circles. It is prescribed for sleepiness, and no appearance effect has been studied.

adrafinil.text: Adrafinil is a modafinil prodrug that users take as an over-the-counter route to the same wakefulness for study and work. It was sold in France for vigilance in older adults, human data are thin, and no appearance use has been studied.

citicoline-cdp-choline.text: Citicoline is a choline source taken as a nootropic for focus and memory. It is studied for stroke and brain injury, and no trial tests it for appearance.

alpha-gpc.text: Alpha-GPC is sold as a cognitive and sports supplement, with lifters using it for focus and training output that could support muscle gain. It is a prescription drug for cognitive decline in Italy, and no appearance outcome has been studied.

huperzine-a.text: Huperzine A is a club-moss extract floated in height-maxxing as a way to raise growth hormone by lowering somatostatin. It is approved for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a nootropic, and no study has tested the height claim, which forum posters also dispute.

bacopa-monnieri.text: Bacopa, or brahmi, is taken as a memory nootropic and for stress, with users stacking it for study. Trials are small and reviews call the cognition evidence inconclusive, and appearance effects are not studied.

ginkgo-biloba.text: Ginkgo is sold for memory and circulation, and some users take it as a general nootropic. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit, and no appearance outcome has been studied.

vinpocetine.text: Vinpocetine is a prescription drug in parts of Europe and a US supplement that users take for memory and focus. Evidence in dementia or stroke is described as unsupported by full reviews, and appearance use is untested.

sulbutiamine.text: Sulbutiamine is prescribed for fatigue in France and sold elsewhere, with users taking it for energy, motivation and mental stamina. Human data are sparse and no appearance outcome has been studied.

pyritinol.text: Pyritinol is approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment and sold in the US as a nootropic for memory and focus. Evidence is dated and mixed, and it has no appearance angle tested.

meclofenoxate-centrophenoxine.text: Centrophenoxine is promoted as an anti-aging nootropic, a reputation built on 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan claim. People tie that to looking younger, but no study has examined skin.

bromantane.text: Bromantane is a Russian stimulant-anxiolytic that users take for motivation and lower social stress, and some claim it raises testosterone for physique gains. Human data are small and mostly Russian-language, and the physique claim is anecdotal.

phosphatidylserine.text: Phosphatidylserine is sold for memory and in sports products for recovery from exercise stress, which lifters tie to training harder. Trials are mainly in cognition, with none for appearance.

dimethylaminoethanol-dmae.text: DMAE is an ingredient in skin-firming creams marketed for a tighter, smoother look, and is also sold as a nootropic. No human trial isolates its skin effect.
